title: Edwin Lowe sent to Muileann bheag
summary: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sends the cleric Edwin Lowe up from Ros dhomhain to look into a complaint laid by the keepers of the new beacon at Muileann bheag. He rides three days by mule-track and a fourth along the open coast, and finds the beacon burning coal, the first of the island's lights to do so.

title: Ailig mac Griogair shows Lowe the coloured water
summary: The keeper Ailig mac Griogair takes Lowe up the beacon stair and points out a green colour he says lies on the water beneath the flame, further than the beam itself should carry. Lowe looks a long while and sees only firelight on the swell, and writes that he cannot see what the keeper sees.

title: The keeper's son answers Lowe on the point
summary: Ailig's young son stands the watch beside Lowe on two further nights and tells him the colour is not a thing looked for but a thing seen, as rain is felt before it falls. Lowe records the boy's answer as the most honest, and the least useful, given him in eleven years on the island.

title: The dig opened at Làrach an Teampaill
summary: Lowe opens the ground inside the western wall of Làrach an Teampaill with six labourers of A' Chompanaidh off the Doire ghlas coal contracts, watched by the custodian Griogal Odhar. In the first week they uncover worked stone in even courses, carried from no quarry of the district, below a century of turf.

title: The shepherds of Àth mhòr turn their flocks off the mound
summary: Before the digging begins the shepherds of Àth mhòr move their flocks off the mound of Làrach an Teampaill, which they have grazed every other season, saying only that it is the custom to keep beasts from a grave while the grave stands open.

title: Tormod Ruadh sets down his spade
summary: The eldest of Lowe's labourers, Tormod Ruadh, refuses to dig further once burnt bone is found beside the altar stone, saying he will cut coal for his wage but not dig a man from his own grave for a stranger's paper. The rest of the crew stop with him.

title: Four custodians view the pit at Làrach an Teampaill
summary: Custodians of Doire ghlas, Doire fhiadhaich and Àth mhòr walk out together to the opened pit, judge that the stone, the bone and the flints beside it are of no people or craft they know, and have Lowe cover the pit again with the word said over any grave whose kin cannot be found.

title: Griogal Odhar on Mòd and the older ground
summary: Asked whether any order of the island's faiths claims the ruin, Griogal Odhar tells Lowe that Mòd himself is said not to claim ground older than the vein, for a god who eats the hill can only eat what grew in the hill's own time. No order has ever asked for the ground, and none has been refused it.

title: Lowe copies Colbh Cnoc chiar
summary: Lowe spends nine days rubbing the weathered pillar near Cnoc chiar, watched daily by an old woman of the town carding wool at its foot, who tells him the stone had a name once that nobody now carries, and that this does not mean the stone minds.

title: Lowe sets the pillar beside Wren's obelisk
summary: Lowe lays his rubbing of the Cnoc chiar pillar beside Samuel Wren's old copy of Carragh Cnoc bheag and judges the two hands are not the same, though something in the shapes of both puts him in mind of a single idea, as two strangers' faces can share an expression without sharing a feature.

title: Lowe copies Calbh Cnoc ghorm
summary: Lowe copies Calbh Cnoc ghorm in four days, less worn than the pillar. He writes that the three markers were likely raised by one people at different times, each needing to say less than the last because by then all who read it already knew.

title: Lowe sails for home
summary: Edwin Lowe takes ship at Ros dhomhain the year after copying Calbh Cnoc ghorm, his notebooks sealed under his berth. No answer is ever recorded as coming back over the sea to the stone he copied or the bone he uncovered and covered again.

title: Voss stays behind at Baile Mòr dhìreach
summary: When his glazing of A' Chompanaidh contract ends, Peter Voss does not take passage home, telling the muster clerk only that he has found white sand below Baile Mòr dhìreach the like of which he never found in three counties of an Tìr Thall, and means to see what it will make in a furnace.

title: The first three firings give only slag
summary: Voss's first three firings of white sand and charcoal give only a black glassy slag, which the town's children carry off for luck and the custodians' clerk records as Voss's first stones, being none. Voss breaks each batch himself and changes the fire and the sand before trying again.

title: Cairistìona nic Griogair sees the first pane
summary: Voss's fourth firing gives a pale green pane clear enough to see a gull through. His apprentice Cairistìona nic Griogair, who carried sand for him all that summer, laughs at the sight of it, the first laugh heard in the glass-house yard since the furnace was raised.

title: Martha Gale reads the partnership at Muileann chiar
summary: Martha Gale brings A' Chompanaidh's offer of partnership to Comann an Airgid hall at Muileann chiar. A clerk reads it in the humans' tongue and a guild boy puts it into Dia-thìris sentence by sentence, at Ùna nic Choinnich's insistence, so that no hand voting on it can say it did not understand.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich questions A' Chompanaidh's beam
summary: Ùna nic Choinnich, some eighty winters old, has the paragraph on A' Chompanaidh's weighing-beam read a third time and asks twice what the weight would be measured against, unsatisfied with the clerk's answers both times, before putting the offer to the guild's hands.

title: The guild's hands refuse the partnership
summary: The guild hall at Muileann chiar refuses A' Chompanaidh's partnership by every hand but one, an old silversmith too deaf that year to have followed the second reading. Martha Gale takes the count without argument and thanks the hall in a careful, correct Dia-thìris never heard from her again.

title: The camp opened at Achadh dhomhain
summary: A' Chompanaidh opens the deep galleries below the hill at Achadh dhomhain, and within a season the old farming village finds itself the largest gathering of people on that stretch of coast, though it has no market, no charter and no custodian of its own.

title: Dùn chiar votes to weave for the camps
summary: The town council of Dùn chiar votes twenty-six to nine to take a contract of A' Chompanaidh for camp canvas, against the eldest weaver Ealasaid Bhuidhe, who signs the roll of dissent and then weaves canvas with the rest once the custodian has ruled.

title: Cormag mac Ailein raises the first house of spoil
summary: The hewer Cormag mac Ailein builds the first house of Achadh dhomhain's camp from stacked spoil chinked with clay and roofs it with Dùn chiar's first bolts of canvas before the frost, tarring the seams himself, his household under it before the year's shortest day.
